positions.decision: A

topic: Garage CSVExportService currently mangles data (replaces commas with spaces/semicolons, no quoting) and has a spreadsheet formula-injection vector. Which export policy?

positions.decision: A
positions.reasoning: RFC-4180 quoting fixes the data-mangling losslessly. Formula injection (=,+,-,@ prefixes) is a real OWASP-documented CSV vector; relying on spreadsheet-app protections (B) is inconsistent across Excel/LibreOffice versions. Scoping the quote-prefix to free-text fields avoids corrupting typed negative numbers, addressing the main objection to blanket neutralization.

positions.decision: A: Full RFC-4180 quoting (preserve data exactly; quote fields containing comma/quote/newline, double embedded quotes) + OWASP formula-injection neutralization (prefix leading = + - @ with a single quote) applied ONLY to free-text fields - numeric columns are emitted from typed numbers and stay unprefixed, preserving negatives
positions.reasoning: The prompt establishes two defects: lossy, non-quoted CSV serialization and a formula-injection vector. A fixes both while preserving exact text through RFC-4180 escaping. Restricting neutralization to free-text fields avoids corrupting typed numeric values, especially legitimate negatives. B knowingly leaves the security flaw; C preserves both defects.

positions.decision: A
positions.reasoning: Option A resolves both data mangling and injection vulnerabilities. Using RFC-4180 ensures data integrity, while selectively applying OWASP mitigations to free-text fields prevents formula injection without corrupting legitimate negative numeric values.
